cards.q: Benefits of making a drug act longer
cards.a: Fewer doses, better compliance, fewer peak side effects, smoother levels, overnight cover

cards.q: Half-life below which controlled-release forms are suitable
cards.a: Under 4 hours

cards.q: Half-life above which controlled-release is not needed
cards.a: Over 12 hours

cards.q: Drugs that are already long-acting and need no controlled release: examples
cards.a: Doxycycline, omeprazole, digoxin, amlodipine

cards.q: Brief-acting drugs that do not need prolonging: examples
cards.a: Sleep-inducing hypnotic; headache remedy

cards.q: Select patient groups that benefit from controlled-release forms
cards.a: Patients on antiepileptic or antipsychotic agents

cards.q: Methods of prolonging drug action (KDT8): list the four
cards.a: Slower absorption from site; increased plasma protein binding; retarded metabolism; retarded renal excretion

cards.q: Prolonging action by slowing metabolism: example
cards.a: Ethinyl group added to oestradiol (ethinyl oestradiol) for oral contraceptives

cards.q: Enzyme inhibition prolonging another drug: examples
cards.a: Allopurinol with 6-mercaptopurine; ritonavir boosting atazanavir, lopinavir, saquinavir; cilastatin with imipenem

cards.q: Probenecid: effect on penicillin and how
cards.a: Prolongs penicillin, ampicillin and amoxicillin action by blocking tubular secretion

cards.q: Congener highly bound to plasma protein: example
cards.a: Sulfadoxine, slowly released in free active form

cards.q: Vasoconstrictor added to injected drug: effect
cards.a: Delays absorption (e.g. adrenaline with local anaesthetics)

cards.q: Subcutaneous insulin absorption: how the rate is varied
cards.a: Particle size, protein complexation and pH of the preparation

cards.q: Drugs whose absorption can be deliberately delayed: overdose consequence (modified release)
cards.a: Absorption delayed and prolonged, so toxicity may appear late or last longer

cards.q: Sustained-release tablets: how they work
cards.a: Particles coated with materials that dissolve at different rates, spreading absorption

cards.q: Controlled-release tablets: how they work
cards.a: Semipermeable membrane controls drug release

cards.q: Duration extended from 2-6 hours by sustained release to
cards.a: 12 hours or more

cards.q: Controlled-release tablet: release pattern
cards.a: About 30% released at once; 70% released slowly through the membrane over 4-8 hours

cards.q: Limit of oral sustained- or controlled-release action
cards.a: Only 4-8 hours, as particles reach the colon

cards.q: Oral sustained-release drawback for blood levels
cards.a: Release and blood levels more variable than a regular tablet

cards.q: Spansule
cards.a: Extended-release capsule packed with granules having different coatings that dissolve over time

cards.q: Enteric-coated capsule dissolves where
cards.a: Ileum

cards.q: Problems of oral therapy overcome by enteric-coated and sustained-release forms
cards.a: Acid lability, gastric irritancy and short duration of action

cards.q: Drug destroyed by gastric acid (oral example)
cards.a: Penicillin G

cards.q: Enteric coating: best uses (GG14)
cards.a: Drugs causing gastric irritation; delivering drugs to ileum or colon (e.g. mesalamine)

cards.q: Mesalazine: coat and site of release
cards.a: pH-dependent acrylic coat; degrades in terminal ileum and proximal colon

cards.q: Olsalazine: structure and where it is activated
cards.a: Dimer of two 5-aminosalicylic acid molecules; cleaved by colonic bacteria

cards.q: Capsule or tablet designed to delay absorption
cards.a: Capsule that stays intact for hours, or tablet with resistant coating

cards.q: Capsule with mixed slow and fast particles: intended effect
cards.a: Rapid but sustained absorption

cards.q: Modified-release preparations: two advantages
cards.a: Less frequent dosing; fewer adverse effects from high peak concentrations

cards.q: Oral vancomycin: why it is given by mouth
cards.a: Very poorly absorbed; acts in gut lumen against C. difficile

cards.q: Digoxin tablet formulations: outcome of variation study
cards.a: Large variation in absorption; tablet formulation later standardised

cards.q: Depot injections in insoluble or oily form: examples
cards.a: Benzathine penicillin, lente insulin (insoluble); depot progestins such as medroxyprogesterone (oily solution)

cards.q: Parenteral depot and implant absorption span
cards.a: A couple of days to several months, even years

cards.q: Pellet implantation: how inserted and release period
cards.a: Solid pellet inserted with trocar and cannula; release over weeks to months

cards.q: Drugs given as subcutaneous pellets: examples
cards.a: DOCA, testosterone (KDT8); oestradiol (RangDale9)

cards.q: Pellet implant: what sets its absorption rate
cards.a: Surface area of the implant (rate proportional to it)

cards.q: Non-biodegradable vs biodegradable implant: removal
cards.a: Non-biodegradable must be removed later; biodegradable does not

cards.q: Contraceptive implant named in KDT8
cards.a: Norplant

cards.q: Dermojet: what it is and main use
cards.a: Needle-free gun firing a high-velocity drug jet into subcutaneous tissue; nearly painless, for mass inoculation

cards.q: Subcutaneous injection: drugs allowed
cards.a: Only non-irritating drugs

cards.q: Subcutaneous route: pattern of absorption
cards.a: Generally constant and slow, giving a sustained effect

cards.q: Subcutaneous route to avoid in patients
cards.a: Shock (vasoconstriction delays absorption)

cards.q: Intramuscular depot vehicles give absorption that is
cards.a: Slow and constant (oily solution or suspension)

cards.q: Transdermal therapeutic system (TTS): what it does
cards.a: Adhesive patch delivering drug at a constant rate into systemic circulation through the stratum corneum

cards.q: TTS patch size
TTS construction
cards.a: Drug reservoir between occlusive backing film and rate-controlling micropore membrane; adhesive with priming dose; protective peel-off film

cards.q: Why TTS gives constant delivery whatever the site
cards.a: Micropore membrane delivers drug slower than the slowest skin absorption rate

cards.q: TTS application sites: list
cards.a: Chest, abdomen, upper arm, lower back, buttock, mastoid region

cards.q: TTS wear duration
cards.a: 1-3 days, depending on drug

cards.q: TTS advantages over tablets
cards.a: Smooth levels; less inter-individual variation; little first-pass metabolism; better compliance

cards.q: TTS limitations
cards.a: More expensive; local irritation (reduced by rotating site)

cards.q: Ways to enhance cutaneous absorption
cards.a: Rubbing, oily base, occlusive dressing

cards.q: Skin absorption depends on
cards.a: Area covered and lipid solubility; much greater through abraded, burned or denuded skin

cards.q: Which drugs suit patch delivery and main cost issue
cards.a: Only lipid-soluble drugs; relatively expensive

cards.q: Controlled-release topical patches (GG14): examples
cards.a: Nicotine, scopolamine, nitroglycerin, testosterone, estrogen and progestins, fentanyl

cards.q: Patches marketed in India (KDT8): list
cards.a: GTN, fentanyl, nicotine, estradiol

cards.q: Peptide drugs given as nasal sprays: list
cards.a: Antidiuretic hormone, GnRH analogues, calcitonin

cards.q: Why nasal route works for peptides
cards.a: Absorption through mucosa over nasal-associated lymphoid tissue, which is unusually permeable

cards.q: Sublingual route: main advantage
cards.a: Venous drainage to vena cava bypasses first-pass metabolism

cards.q: Why sublingual nitroglycerin acts quickly
cards.a: Nonionic, highly lipid-soluble, avoids first-pass effect

cards.q: Drugs given buccally or sublingually: examples
cards.a: Glyceryl trinitrate, buprenorphine, buccal midazolam

cards.q: Rectal route: share of absorbed drug bypassing the liver
cards.a: About 50%

cards.q: Rectal route: reliability and drawbacks
cards.a: Irregular, incomplete; can irritate rectal mucosa

cards.q: Rectal route: when used in practice
cards.a: When vomiting or unable to take oral drugs, and in hospice care (opioids)

cards.q: Rectal diazepam or paracetamol in children
cards.a: Absorbed rapidly and dependably from the rectum

cards.q: Inhaled corticosteroids and bronchodilators: aim
cards.a: High lung levels with minimal systemic effects

cards.q: Ipratropium: why it is a useful inhaled bronchodilator
cards.a: Quaternary analogue of atropine; poorly absorbed, fewer systemic effects

cards.q: Dorzolamide eye drops: advantage over oral acetazolamide
cards.a: Lowers ocular pressure without renal action, so no acidosis

cards.q: Intravitreal implants for macular oedema
cards.a: Slowly release corticosteroid (fluocinolone or dexamethasone) over months

cards.q: Approaches to localise drugs to target tissue (Rang & Dale): list
cards.a: Prodrugs; antibody-drug conjugates; packaging in liposomes; coated implantable devices

cards.q: Prodrug: definition
cards.a: Inactive precursor metabolised to an active drug

cards.q: Cyclophosphamide as a prodrug: benefit
cards.a: Activated only in the liver, so it can be given orally without gut damage

cards.q: Levodopa: how it reaches the brain
cards.a: Crosses the blood-brain barrier on an amino acid transporter, then converted to dopamine

cards.q: Zidovudine: why it is selectively toxic to HIV-infected cells
cards.a: Phosphorylated to active triphosphate only where the appropriate reverse transcriptase is present

cards.q: Valaciclovir and famciclovir: prodrug type and active drugs
cards.a: Ester prodrugs of aciclovir and penciclovir

cards.q: Aspirin as an early deliberate prodrug: purpose
cards.a: Made as a less gut-irritant prodrug of salicylic acid for oral use

cards.q: Antibody-drug conjugate: principle
cards.a: Cytotoxic drug or toxin attached to an antibody against a tumour-specific antigen

cards.q: FDA-approved antibody-drug conjugates in Rang & Dale: indication
cards.a: Ado-trastuzumab emtansine (metastatic breast cancer); brentuximab vedotin (Hodgkin's lymphoma)

cards.q: Nucleic-acid drugs (antisense, siRNA) delivered to hepatocytes via
cards.a: GalNAc (N-acetylgalactosamine) conjugates

cards.q: Asialoglycoprotein receptor: where found and what it binds
cards.a: Abundant on hepatocytes; binds terminal galactose and GalNAc

cards.q: Liposome: size
cards.a: 0.1-1 micrometre diameter

cards.q: How liposomes are made
cards.a: Sonication of phospholipid (e.g. lecithin) in aqueous suspension

cards.q: Liposomes: which drugs they carry and when released
cards.a: Non-lipid-soluble drugs, retained until the liposome is disrupted

cards.q: Where injected liposomes go
cards.a: Taken up by reticuloendothelial cells, especially liver and spleen; also concentrate in some malignant cells

cards.q: Antibody tagging of liposomes
cards.a: Being tried to target other specific tissues

cards.q: Liposomal amphotericin B: uses (KDT8)
cards.a: Kala-azar and serious systemic mycoses

cards.q: Liposomal amphotericin B: advantage over conventional form
cards.a: Less nephrotoxic and better tolerated, but more expensive

cards.q: Liposomal doxorubicin: indications
cards.a: Ovarian cancer and myeloma

cards.q: Liposomal cytarabine: use
cards.a: Intrathecal treatment of lymphomatous meningitis

cards.q: Albumin nanoparticle paclitaxel: use
cards.a: Breast cancer

cards.q: Newer carriers named by GG14
cards.a: Biocompatible polymers and nanoparticles

cards.q: Drug-eluting coronary stent: purpose
cards.a: Keeps the artery patent after balloon angioplasty; reduces restenosis and angioplasty failure

cards.q: Stent coatings: examples
cards.a: Antithrombotic or antiproliferative agents; sirolimus in a surface polymer

cards.q: Restenosis with drug-coated stents
cards.a: Can still occur at the margin of the device

cards.q: Progestin-impregnated IUCD: duration of protection
cards.a: Up to 5 years

cards.q: Hormone-releasing intrauterine device: site of action
cards.a: Delivers hormone to the endometrium

cards.q: Other devices for local targeting (GG14)
cards.a: Microneedle drug delivery patches; aim is local drug action with minimal systemic exposure

cards.q: Long-acting hormonal contraception from implants or devices (GG14)
cards.a: Implanted or oral controlled-release devices

cards.q: Intrauterine and implanted local hormone release: purpose (KDT8)
cards.a: Drug-releasing implants give prolonged delivery of minute quantities to the target organ
